blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A transformer in service is 30 years old. Its fleet's Weibull curve gives survival R(30) = 0.50 and R(31) = 0.45. Which probability of failure goes into next year's risk?

options.text: 0.55, the share of new units that have failed by age 31
options.says: That is F(31), the chance of having failed by 31 for a unit of unknown history, not a yearly probability.

options.text: 0.05, the share of new units that fail between ages 30 and 31
options.says: That is the unconditional difference; it counts units that already failed, so it understates the risk.

options.text: 0.50, the share of new units that have failed by age 30
options.says: That is F(30), the CDF the trap warns about; the unit is working today.

options.text: 0.10, the share of units still working at 30 that fail by 31
options.says: Right: 1 - R(31)/R(30) = 1 - 0.45/0.50, conditional on the unit working today.

origin.section: Trap Questions: Formulas That Look Right and Are Not

questions.stem: A portfolio has 65 Pareto-optimal plans of NPV against risk removed. You maximize NPV with a risk floor and sweep the floor over 21 values. What does the sweep give you?

options.text: The exact frontier, since a floor returns the plans at that risk
options.says: Each floor returns one plan, so 21 floors cannot return 65 plans.

options.text: At most 21 plans, since a floor returns one plan, maybe a weak one
options.says: Right: 21 floors found 20 of GridCap small's 65, and plain ε-constraint can return weakly efficient plans.

options.text: Supported plans alone, since a floor works like a weight on the risk
options.says: A floor is not a weight: ε-constraint reaches unsupported plans that no weighted sum returns.

options.text: The 65 plans, since floors between the plans return the plans nearby
options.says: A floor returns one plan, and plans between floors are skipped; steps must fit the data.

questions.stem: A $1,000k estimate is in 2026 prices, costs escalate 4% a year and are discounted at 7%, and the project may start in 2027 or 2030. A colleague escalates by 1.04 to the power of the years since the project's start. What happens to the 2030 start?

options.text: Nothing, since the escalation and the discount cancel for each start year
options.says: They cancel only when the two rates are equal; at 4% and 7% the printed values differ.

options.text: It looks dearer than it is, since four years of escalation are added twice
options.says: Counting from the start drops escalation; it adds none. The 2030 start looks cheaper.

options.text: It looks cheaper than it is, since four years before the start are lost
options.says: Right: from 2026 to 2030 is four years of escalation the shortcut never applies; $892.5k becomes $762.9k.

options.text: Nothing, since escalation from either year gives the same present value
options.says: The printed table gives $892.5k from the base year and $762.9k from the start year.
